column2: Arad's king hears of Israel's Atharim route and attacks; the plural captors take prisoners. The wilderness location follows the selected Greek.
Israel's vow conditions devotion to destruction on God's handing over the people. Thou addresses God; the collective speaker uses my.
Divine hearing and delivery precede destruction of people and towns. The place-name translates the selected devotion term.
Israel circles Edom by the Red Sea road, becoming fainthearted on the journey. The route and emotional response remain.
Complaint against God and Moses names no bread or water and disgust with empty bread. The contradictory-sounding food complaint is not rationalized away.
The selected snakes are deadly, not explicitly fiery; their bites kill many Israelites.
The proposal retains the selected singular the serpent in the removal petition. The surrounding plural snakes remain in verse 6; the collective force of the singular here is left available.
Moses is told to make a serpent on a standard, and the bitten person lives by looking. Bronze is not supplied before the next verse states it.
Moses makes the bronze serpent; repeated biting, looking and living describe the result.
The departure ends at Oboth, with the selected stop preserved.
Achel-gai lies beyond, in wilderness facing Moab toward sunrise. The selected place form is not replaced by another itinerary name.
The next camp is in Zered's ravine; the geographic feature remains.
The far side of Arnon, Amorite border extension and Moab/Amorite boundary explanation are all represented.
The quotation begins after in a book; war of the Lord is the quoted subject that burned Zoob, not automatically a book title.
The selected torrent-settlement statement and Moab boundary remain without reconstructing a different poem.
column3: The implicit subject of appointed and the settlement syntax require fuller review; he is provisional.

column2: The well is identified by the Lord's command to assemble people and promise drinking water. It is not replaced by an unexamined place-name.
Israel sings over the well and commands leading its song. A spring-up command from another source is not inserted.
Rulers, kings of nations, kingdom and dominion are all retained in the selected well poem, followed by departure to Manthanain.
The sequence Manthanain, Nahaliel and Bamoth remains in order.
The route leads to a valley in Moab's plain from the Hewn Height summit facing wilderness. The translated height expression remains provisional.
Moses sends envoys to Sihon with explicit words of peace. This selected longer introduction remains.
Road travel excludes fields, vineyards and well water and repeats the royal-road promise until the border is passed.
Sihon refuses, gathers all his people and arrays against Israel in wilderness at Jahaz. The repeated military action remains.
Conquest extends Arnon to Jabbok and Ammon's border. Jazer is explicitly named as the boundary explanation, not replaced by a statement of strength.
Israel takes and inhabits all the towns, with Heshbon and its adjoining towns specified.
Sihon's prior war against Moab explains Heshbon's status; the selected Aroer-to-Arnon extent and plural they took remain.
Riddle-speakers introduce the Heshbon poem, calling for Sihon's city to be built and prepared.
Fire and flame consume as far as Moab and swallow Arnon's pillars. The selected imagery is not replaced by lords of heights.
Moab and Chemosh's people receive the woe; sons are handed over to escape and daughters as captives. The passive and different outcomes remain.
The seed perishes between Heshbon and Dibon; women kindle further fire against Moab in the selected line. No familiar alternative ending is substituted.
Israel's settlement in all Amorite towns repeats the narrative result after the poem.
Inspection, capture of Jazer and villages, and expulsion of resident Amorites remain distinct actions.
The Bashan route meets Og and all his people at Edrei for battle.
The Lord forbids fear and declares Og, people and land delivered, comparing Sihon's defeat. All three delivered objects remain.
The singular victor strikes Og, sons and all people; the plural group then inherits their land. No survivor is left in the selected statement.
Israel camps on Moab's western side beside Jordan opposite Jericho, retaining the selected directional wording.
Balak son of Zippor sees all that Israel did to the Amorites.
Moab fears Israel's numbers and is distressed before them; both reactions remain.
Moab addresses Midian's elders with the calf-and-greenery image. Balak's kingship is located at that time.
Balaam son of Beor is summoned from Pethor by the river; the land-of-his-people phrase remains provisional. The message stresses covering the land and camping nearby.
column3: The compact kinship/geographic phrase needs further syntax and name review.

column2: Balak seeks a curse against a stronger people, hoping to strike and expel them. Blessing and cursing effectiveness are his claims.
Both Moabite and Midianite elders carry means of divination. The ambiguous object is not narrowed to a stated fee without lexical review.
Balaam requests an overnight stay and promises the Lord's answer. The closing residents are specifically Moab's officials.
God asks who the men with Balaam are, without an added motive for the question.
Balaam identifies Balak, his father and kingship before quoting the message.
The repeated message includes nearby encampment and the tentative hope of striking and expelling the people.
God forbids both the journey and the curse because the people are blessed.
Balaam attributes his refusal to God's prohibition and sends officials back to their human lord.
The officials report Balaam's unwillingness; the draft does not add the divine explanation they omit.
Balak sends more officials of higher honour. Both comparative changes remain.
The new delegates relay Balak's personal request not to hesitate.
Emphatic promised honour and compliance precede the renewed curse demand.
Even a house full of silver and gold cannot authorize transgressing the Lord God's word. The selected own-intention clause remains.
A second overnight stay seeks what further word the Lord will give; also you distinguishes the new group.
The permission is conditional on the men's summons and bounded by doing God's stated word. The later anger is not pre-explained here.
Balaam saddles his donkey in the morning and accompanies Moab's officials.
God's anger follows the journey; the angel obstructs Balaam, who rides with two servants. The tension with permission remains unharmonized.
The female donkey sees the drawn sword and turns into the plain; Balaam strikes her to redirect her. The seeing agent is the animal.
The angel stands in vineyard furrows between two fences. No broad road is substituted for this narrowed setting.
The donkey presses against the wall and crushes Balaam's foot, prompting a further whipping.
The angel moves to a place too narrow for turning either right or left. Both blocked directions remain.
The donkey crouches under Balaam, who beats her in anger. No fall or collapse is added.
God opens the donkey's mouth; she asks why this is the third beating. The source's present speech verb is retained.
Balaam alleges mockery and says he would already have stabbed her if armed. The counterfactual remains distinct from the angel's actual sword.
The donkey invokes riding from Balaam's youth and denies deliberate disregard. His no answers that question, not her ownership.
God uncovers Balaam's eyes; he sees the Lord's angel and bows face down. The change from God's angel to Lord's angel remains.
The angel repeats the third-beating question and explains opposition by the unfitting road. The reason is not expanded into an unexpressed intention.
The donkey's threefold turning prevented Balaam's death; the contrasted preservation of her life remains.
Balaam confesses sin and ignorance of the angel's opposition, offering to return if displeasing. Ordinary you addresses the angel without an added divine identity.
The angel permits companionship but restricts speech to the given word. Balaam then goes with Balak's officials.
Balak meets Balaam at a Moabite city on the Arnon frontier. The city is not assigned an unexpressed name.
Balak's three questions concern summons, delay and ability to honour. The rhetorical denial of inability remains.
Balaam affirms arrival but limits speech to what God puts in his mouth.
The selected plural towns of farmsteads remains rather than an imported singular proper place-name.
Balak sacrifices sheep and calves and sends portions to Balaam and the officials. Portions supplies the natural object of sent from the sacrificial context.
Balak brings Balaam to Baal's pillar and shows a part of the people. Neither the monument nor the limited view is generalized into another source's wording.
